title: Amazon Wants 1,000 Same-Day Delivery Hubs Within 10 Miles of Prime Members
excerpt: Codenamed Project Mercury, the internal plan would grow Amazon's same-day footprint from 85 sites to more than 1,000 by 2031, placing hubs within a 10-mile radius of 80% of US Prime subscribers. Amazon says the projections are preliminary and subject to revision.
body:
• Amazon is planning an internal initiative, codenamed Project Mercury, to expand its same-day delivery network from about 85 facilities to more than 1,000 sites by 2031, according to internal planning documents cited by Business Insider.
  • The plan would place same-day hubs within a 10-mile radius of 80% of US Prime subscribers — down from today's roughly 90-minute driving distance.
  • Amazon's three-year operating plan allocates $6.8 billion for US same-day delivery capacity in 2026 and 2027; an internal analysis estimates the project could generate $7.1 billion in economic value over a decade and turn cash-flow positive by 2030.
  • An Amazon spokesperson cautioned that the internal projections are "preliminary, subject to significant revision, and shouldn't be treated as finalized plans."

What Amazon is planning

Amazon is weighing the most ambitious overhaul of its US logistics network since the Prime two-day era, according to internal planning documents reviewed by Business Insider. The initiative, codenamed Project Mercury, would grow the company's same-day fulfillment footprint from roughly 85 sites today to more than 1,000 by 2031.

The redesign hinges on distance. Amazon currently positions many same-day sites about a 90-minute drive from customers; Mercury would rebuild the network around a 10-mile straight-line radius covering 80% of US Prime subscribers by 2031. The strategy centers on stocking a narrower range of fast-moving inventory — fresh food, paper towels, cough medicine — in small facilities close to where people live.

Amazon's finance team has evaluated the economics of the project, with operations chief Udit Madan involved in the planning, according to the report.

Why speed is the strategy

Same-day delivery has become the engine of Amazon's push into everyday spending. Doug Herrington, CEO of Worldwide Amazon Stores, has said that when Amazon speeds up delivery, "the probability that somebody buys a product from us goes up. And what's even more interesting is that if they buy it, they're going to come back sooner, and they're going to shop more when they do."

"The probability that somebody buys a product from us goes up. And what's even more interesting is that if they buy it, they're going to come back sooner, and they're going to shop more when they do."

— Doug Herrington, CEO of Worldwide Amazon Stores

The early data backs him up. Since the start of the year, the number of monthly active customers buying perishables has risen more than 50%, and same-day orders containing perishables carry three times as many units on average, CEO Andy Jassy said on the company's second-quarter earnings call. Faster delivery doesn't just win the order — it grows the basket.

The target also closes a gap with Walmart, the one rival Amazon can't outrun on proximity: roughly 90% of the US population lives within 10 miles of a Walmart or Sam's Club store, and the retailer can deliver orders to 95% of US households in less than three hours. Mercury would give Amazon a comparable physical footprint in the suburbs where the grocery wars are being won. For diaspora families who rely on Amazon for everything from weekly groceries to festival-season essentials, a 10-mile same-day radius would narrow the last real advantage of the neighborhood store.

The economics

The plan is not cheap. Amazon's three-year operating plan allocates $6.8 billion for US same-day delivery capacity in 2026 and 2027 alone. But the company's internal analysis estimates Project Mercury could generate $7.1 billion in economic value over a decade and reach positive cash flow by 2030 — partly because some of the new investment would replace spending on traditional delivery facilities rather than adding to it.

Internal forecasts show Amazon expects same-day hubs to handle 28% of company-fulfilled volume by 2029 and 50% by 2035, with 94% of same-day packages delivered within five hours of the order by 2029, according to the documents.

What's next

Amazon isn't confirming the plan. A company spokesperson told Business Insider that internal projections are "preliminary, subject to significant revision, and shouldn't be treated as finalized plans," while noting that its same-day service already reaches more than 10,000 cities and towns, including rural areas, even though not all same-day orders move through dedicated facilities.

"Internal projections are preliminary, subject to significant revision, and shouldn't be treated as finalized plans."

— Amazon spokesperson, in a statement to Business Insider

Still, the numbers point in one direction: delivery speed is becoming the decisive battlefield in American retail, and Amazon intends to fight it on Walmart's home turf. Whether the 1,000-hub blueprint survives the finance team's revisions, the signal to competitors has already been sent.
